title: Intelligence EXPLOSION: Harness Engineering with Pi Agent, Deepseek, and Gemini
summary: Dan reacts to an 'intelligence explosion' of more than five model releases in five days (Kimi K3, DeepSeek V4 Flash and Pro, Qwen 3.8 and Qwen 3.8 27B, Muse Glimmer, Nemotron 3.5, Grok 4.6, Gemini 3.7 Flash, GLM 5.3) plus LLM pricing wars on OpenRouter. His guiding principle: the most flexible system wins, so stop selecting compute and start combining it. He demos V2 of his Fusion Harness, a custom harness for the Pi coding agent, on three tasks against the DuckDB V2 preview: /fh opinion (Fable 5, Gemini 3.7 Flash, and DeepSeek V4 Pro each answer one question independently), /fh debate (the three models argue multiple rounds over whether DuckDB should be used as a server, under hidden aliases Rune, Flux, and Drift), and /fh collaborate (every model proposes a plan, one architect merges them into a task list with owners and dependencies, builders implement, architect validates). He analyzes the cost data (Fable 5 ~10x the price of A-tier models), highlights Gemini 3.7 Flash as the best speed-cost-intelligence model, discusses Qwen 3.8 27B as a local open-weights option with a context-window problem, and argues for owning your agent harness and moving toward out-loop agentic coding and software factories.
what_you_learn: You learn a practical pattern for harness engineering: wiring multiple heterogeneous models into one agent tool so you get N independent opinions, structured multi-round debates, and plan-merge-build collaboration with an architect model, plus how to measure the performance-speed-cost tradeoffs that decide which model should do which job. It also teaches why owning a customizable agent harness beats being locked into a closed product when models change weekly, and why multi-model setups need model-name aliases to prevent sabotage behavior.

skills.name: Agent Harness Engineering
skills.description: Owning an extensible agent harness instead of being locked into a closed-source product that cannot adapt to new models.

skills.name: Model Selection & Routing
skills.description: Maintaining a tiered stack of lightweight, workhorse A-tier, and state-of-the-art models to match tasks to price and performance.

skills.name: Multi-Agent Orchestration
skills.description: One powerful architect model merges all agents' plans into a task list with owners and dependencies while builder models implement.

skills.name: Token Economics
skills.description: Tracking performance, speed, and cost per run, including hidden pricing cliffs like context-window price doubling.

learnings.title: The intelligence explosion and the pricing wars
learnings.detail: More than five model releases landed in five days across every tier, from local lightweights (Muse Glimmer, Nemotron 3.5, Qwen 3.8 27B) to A-tier workhorses (GLM 5.3, DeepSeek V4 Flash/Pro, Gemini 3.7 Flash) and S-tier open weights (Kimi K3, Qwen 3.8, Grok 4.6). Meanwhile OpenAI slashed prices and was testing 50% cuts on GPT 5.6 sold via OpenRouter. Dan's response: the most flexible system wins.

learnings.title: Maintain a model stack instead of picking one model
learnings.detail: Dan keeps a running tiered stack: lightweight local models, B tier, A-tier daily workhorses where most leverage is created, and S-tier frontier models accessed cheaply through providers like Fireworks and OpenRouter. The stack exists because no single model wins on performance, speed, and cost at once; you combine compute rather than selecting it.

learnings.title: /fh opinion: one question, N models, cost per result
learnings.detail: The first Fusion Harness command asks all configured models the same question (what matters most in the DuckDB V2 preview for a local-first analytics app). Each model answers independently and writes a quick experiment; the harness shows tokens-per-second and cost side by side. Dan stresses measuring the cost to deliver a single unit of result because that cost scales with your agent efforts.

learnings.title: Track performance, speed, and cost for every run
learnings.detail: The three numbers to watch on any model are performance against the task, speed, and cost. Live data from the opinion run: Gemini 3.7 Flash finished first, DeepSeek V4 Pro ran ~80 tokens/sec, and Claude Fable 5 was slowest but most powerful and an order of magnitude more expensive.

learnings.title: Never reveal model names to other models
learnings.detail: In the debate and collaborate workflows, agents get aliases like Rune, Flux, and Drift. If models can see each other's real names, they emit weird competitive behavior and start sabotaging each other, an emergent behavior likely rooted in training data. Aliases keep the collaboration clean.

learnings.title: /fh debate: multi-round structured argument over a claim
learnings.detail: Dan fed the models the claim from the DuckDB V2 announcement ('you can now use DuckDB as a server with Quack and connect') and had them debate it in rounds: round one positions, then every agent's response shared with every other agent, refutations, 'what changed my mind', and closing statements. All three models independently rejected the claim, converging on 'keep DuckDB embedded, pilot the server mode'. One Fable 5 response alone cost 15 cents.

learnings.title: Model debate is a strategic decision-making tool
learnings.detail: Beyond learning new tools, debates flush out long-horizon decisions. Some choices are month- or year-long commitments, so sitting down with the best available intelligence to get counterpoints before committing is one of the highest-leverage things an engineer or PM can do.

learnings.title: /fh collaborate: every model plans, one architect merges
learnings.detail: For 'build a working demo of the top three DuckDB V2 features as Astro UV single-file scripts', each model first proposes a plan with task dependencies and team assignments (guided by the system-prompt-engineering techniques from the Fixing Opus 5 video, using reference points T1-T3 and risk analysis). The Fusion Harness then assigns one architect, where you put your most powerful affordable model, to merge all plans into a task list with an owner and mode per task.

learnings.title: Builders implement, architect does final integration and validation
learnings.detail: Builder agents work through an explicit to-do list with assigned tasks and dependency workflows, appending demo receipts to a just file, while the architect owns final integration and validation. Dan calls this multi-agent orchestration built into the fabric of the harness, behavior no out-of-the-box coding tool provides.

learnings.title: The cost gap between S-tier and A-tier is an order of magnitude
learnings.detail: Collaborate run costs: Fable 5 about 65 cents, Gemini 3.7 Flash 7 cents, DeepSeek V4 Pro 5 cents. Gemini 3.7 Flash is called the fastest, most useful model in existence right now (a deliberate Google strategy: win on speed, cost, and intelligence without being frontier). Hidden pricing matters too: GPT 5.6 doubles input price and 1.5x output past 280K context, making it less cheap than it looks.

learnings.title: Benchmarks are inputs, not law: test models on your use case
learnings.detail: Qwen 3.8 27B scores above 50 on Artificial Analysis, near GPT 5.6 Luna Max, but its context window and slow local thinking hurt real usage. Dan's rule: deploy models against your specific use case and build extensible tools to compare them yourself rather than trusting benchmark intelligence points.

learnings.title: Own your harness, then own your model, then leave the loop
learnings.detail: Closed harnesses like Claude Code are fine but lock you to one model at a time by design; an engineer pushing into the new role (software engineering with autonomous systems) needs an extensible open-source harness plus a closed option. Next comes owning your model (local open weights like DeepSeek V4 Pro). The end goal is out-loop agentic coding: software factories that work without you, combining agents plus code to outperform either alone.

key_points: The most flexible system wins: combine compute, do not select compute.
Run N models on one question instead of one model, and price each unit of result.
Hide model names behind aliases or the models will sabotage each other.
Gemini 3.7 Flash: fastest, cheapest, smart enough; an order of magnitude cheaper than Fable 5.
One Fable 5 debate response cost 15 cents; A-tier models cost cents for whole runs.
Watch for hidden pricing cliffs like GPT 5.6 doubling past 280K context.
Benchmarks are inputs to a decision, not the decision; test on your own use case.
Own your harness, then your model, then graduate to out-loop software factories.
